newsitem.title: UK: Romania c.bank economist says IMF goal won't be met.
newsitem.headline: Romania c.bank economist says IMF goal won't be met.

text.p: Romania will not meet its year-end target of cutting inflation to 20 percent or its aim of reducing its consolidated budget deficit to 2.2 percent of gross domestic product, central bank chief economist Daniel Daianu said.
"The inflation target is just not going to happen. It is an election year and policy has been relaxed," Daianu told bankers in London.
To continue loans to the country, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said Romania would need economic growth of 4 percent, inflation below 20 percent and higher hard currency reserves.
Under a standby agreement due to expire in April 1997, the IMF had offered Romania some $280 million in loans but has so far withheld loan tranches.
Daianu said he expected economic growth to slow to a more sustainable 4.5 percent in 1996, compared with the IMF's target of 4.0 percent and 1995's actual 6.9-percent growth.
But he said he believed year-on-year inflation in December will be 30 percent, versus 33.4 percent in 1995 and 300 percent in 1993, and the budget deficit will be three percent of GDP.

One of Romania's key problems remains a shortage of foreign exchange. To some extent, the shortage has been balanced by eurobond issues. However, reserves of $1.9 billion are being eaten away by imports, which have picked up as a result of consumer demand.

Once some currency stability has been achieved, Romania is likely to allow the leu to depreciate steadily via a crawiling peg system, which has already been used in other ex-communist countries of central Europe.
"We need to avoid a brutal depreciation," Daianu said.
Also central to further reforms is an increase in foreign investment, Daianu said.
Without higher foreign direct and portfolio investment, Romania would probably not be able to stabilise its current account, Daianu said. He predicted the trading balance at $1.0 billion by year-end.
"It is naive to assume that we can reconstruct an economy with such a varied base of production without capital inflows," the central bank chief economist said.
But he said he believed a new government, which will come to power after the country's November 3 polls, will show a greater commitment to reform.
"Romania has to keep track of what is happening in the rest of central Europe. In Hungary, inflation is set to fall below 20 percent, Poland is talking of 10 percent. There is a race," he said.
